claims.statement: src/main.rs is the crate's single binary target (oxyromon); it assembles the clap Command from every feature module's subcommand(), appends mcp::subcommand() and server::subcommand() only under their Cargo features, and takes name/version/description/author from CARGO_* compile-time variables so Cargo.toml is the source of truth for --help and --version.

All global startup is gated behind a matched subcommand: with no subcommand on the argv, main() returns Ok without loading .env, installing the logger, creating the data directory, or opening the database pool.

dotenvy's dotenv().ok() runs after argv parsing but before the logger and data-directory lookup, so a .env file in the working directory can supply OXYROMON_LOG_LEVEL, OXYROMON_DATA_DIRECTORY, OXYROMON_ROM_DIRECTORY and OXYROMON_TMP_DIRECTORY to the run.

The logger is built from OXYROMON_LOG_LEVEL with its filter level captured before env_logger is wrapped by indicatif_log_bridge's LogWrapper over the global MultiProgress, then re-applied with log::set_max_level so log records route through the progress UI without losing the configured verbosity.

Startup resolves the data directory through config::get_data_directory (OXYROMON_DATA_DIRECTORY, else platform data dir + /oxyromon), creates it and oxyromon.db if absent, and establishes the pool on that file; establish_connection applies the SQLite pragmas and runs the embedded migrations and panics if either fails.

get_rom_directory and get_tmp_directory are called at startup with their return values discarded, purely so their first-run defaults (OXYROMON_ROM_DIRECTORY or ~/Emulation; OXYROMON_TMP_DIRECTORY or the system temp dir) are written into the settings table for every later lookup.

Pool sizing is feature-conditional: a plain CLI build gets max_connections = 1 with PRAGMA locking_mode = EXCLUSIVE, while any build with the server or mcp feature gets 5 connections with NORMAL locking; both use a 5-second acquire_timeout, so on the CLI pool a second acquire while the running subcommand holds the only connection times out rather than succeeding.

CLI dispatch happens inside a bare block holding the single acquired pooled connection so it is returned to the pool before optimize_database acquires one; optimize_database runs incremental_vacuum, optimize and wal_checkpoint(truncate) on the pool.

The long-lived servers are dispatched after the scoped CLI block and receive pool.clone() instead of a connection, so the server's 5-connection pool starts uncontended; their main() returns only when the transport ends (stdin close or Ctrl+C/SIGTERM for mcp, Ctrl+C/SIGTERM for server), making the entrypoint's optimize_database a shutdown checkpoint. server::shutdown_signal also optimizes the database itself before cancelling in-flight work.
The dispatch match in main.rs terminates in `_ => ()`, so a subcommand registered in the subcommands vec but missing from the match exits silently with success instead of erroring.

Every feature module exports the same contract: pub fn subcommand() -> Command declaring only the argv shape, and pub async fn main(&mut SqliteConnection, &ArgMatches, &ProgressBar) -> anyhow::Result<()>; info omits the matches parameter because its Command declares no arguments, and mcp/server deliberately take a SqlitePool instead of a connection.

Batch subcommands share one selection rule: if --system is given, systems are resolved by name-glob through resolve_systems_by_name_like (sorted and deduped by id so overlapping patterns cannot process a system twice); otherwise prompt_for_systems runs an interactive fuzzy multiselect, bypassed when --all is set or no systems were found.

Interactive prompts are the contract's only TTY dependency: destructive modules expose -y/--yes to short-circuit confirm(), and cfg!(test) is passed as the select-all flag to prompt_for_games so headless runs never block on a multiselect.

The shared progress bar is created once at startup with the none style and passed into every subcommand, which owns it thereafter: it may restyle it, set length and message, tick it, and finish it (info ends the run with finish_and_clear itself), while all user-facing output goes through the categorized print_* helpers on that bar.

The subcommand contract lets non-CLI hosts reuse the same code paths: GraphQL mutations build argv strings, parse them with <module>::subcommand().try_get_matches_from, and run <module>::main inside spawn_cli_action, which acquires its own pooled connection in a spawned task and emits {prefix}_started/_complete/_error over SSE — reporting an acquire failure as an SSE error rather than a panic.

MCP write tools invoke the same subcommand mains through run_action, which takes the shared write lock, acquires a pooled connection, and hands the work a hidden progress bar that a ~400ms poller samples into MCP notifications/progress; because no TTY can answer confirm(), the host-synthesized argv carries the confirmation flag — --yes for the MCP tools, -y for the GraphQL mutations.

Because subcommand() is a standalone argv parser and main() needs only a connection, matches and a bar, tests drive the real pipeline without a CLI harness: temp database via establish_connection, TempDir-backed ROM/tmp settings via the test-only setters, argv through subcommand().get_matches_from, then assertions on database and filesystem state, serialized by the global MUTEX.

Adding a subcommand is a fixed contract: create src/<name>.rs, implement subcommand() and async main(connection, matches, progress_bar), declare the module in src/main.rs, append it to the subcommands vec, add its match arm, and put tests in src/<name>/test_*.rs wired with #[cfg(test)] mod test_*; at the module bottom.

Registering a subcommand touches three separate places in src/main.rs and each omission fails differently: a missing `mod` declaration is a compile error, a missing entry in the `subcommands` vec makes the name unknown to clap (--help/--version), and a missing dispatch arm exits silently with success because the match ends in `_ => ()`.

Non-CLI hosts reuse the subcommand mains by building argv that also suppresses interactive selection, not only confirmation: `--all`/`--system <name>` replaces the system multiselect, `-u/--unattended` narrows import-roms matching, and the axum upload handlers build argv and call import_roms::main / import_irds::main directly instead of routing through the GraphQL mutation layer.

The CLI registers nineteen always-available subcommands — info, config, create-dats, import-dats, download-dats, import-irds, import-patches, import-keys, import-roms, purge-irds, sort-roms, convert-roms, export-roms, rebuild-roms, check-roms, purge-roms, purge-systems, generate-playlists, benchmark — each with a matching dispatch arm, plus the feature-gated mcp (--read-only exposes non-mutating tools only) and server (--address defaults 127.0.0.1, --port defaults 8000).

The `info` subcommand takes no arguments and prints two sections on the shared bar: a Dependencies table built from eight format modules' get_version() (sevenz-rust2, chd-rs, cia-rs, xps-rs, xso-rs, nsz-rs, xdelta-rs, wux-rs) plus `nod` (sourced from rvz, which also backs WBFS), sorted alphabetically by reported name so display order is independent of push order, and a Statistics section of count_systems/count_games/count_roms.

Every dependency in the info table is a compiled-in library reporting `built-in`, with nsz-rs and wux-rs appending a note when their keys file is missing (`prod.keys not found`, `no Wii U keys imported`); ctrtool, the last external subprocess, was replaced by the cia-rs crate behind src/cia.rs.

A dependency whose version call returns Err would be reported as a dim `<name>: not found` line via print_skip, but no format module's get_version() returns an error any more, so `info` never reports a missing dependency.

The nsz-rs entry is the only dependency line that can carry a warning alongside `built-in`: it never fails, but reports `built-in, prod.keys not found` when ~/.switch/prod.keys is absent, surfacing the missing Switch keys at `info` time instead of during NCA compression.

import-keys merges Wii U keys files in Cemu's keys.txt format into wiiu_keys.txt in the data directory, keeping each key once, written owner-only and renamed into place, outside the database so the GraphQL and MCP surfaces cannot return keys.
